title: Onboard a new project as a shelf consumer + beads, in one adaptive verified pass
description:
**Problem.** Onboarding a new project as a shelf consumer *with beads* means reading three
documents that never reference each other — `docs/consuming-the-shelf.md`,
`docs/runbooks/onboard-a-consumer.md` (Phase A duplicates most of it), and
`docs/runbooks/adopt-beads.md` — and getting an ordering right that **none of them states**: the
commit guard must be installed before `bd init`, or bd seizes `core.hooksPath` and the guard is
installed dead (shelf-efh).

`docs/missions/onboarding-new-micro-software.md:44` declares the consumer half **DONE**. It
isn't. What exists describes the destination, not a path to it.

**The crux that reshapes the plan:** `make bootstrap` (shelf-abf) cannot bootstrap greenfield —
it assumes a Makefile that onboarding itself is supposed to produce. Something has to run before
the target repo has anything, which is the precedent `tools/hooks/install.py` already sets: a
program living in shelf, run in the consumer's root.

**Shape of a fix — the governing decision is a split by kind of knowledge.** Onboarding must be
adaptive (greenfield vs established, husky vs pre-commit vs nothing, beads or not, Python or
not), and adaptivity is what a skill is for. But a skill is prose, and this session's whole
lesson is that prose cannot enforce ordering or verification — a skill walking an agent through
ordered steps is the same failure in a new file.

So: **the skill decides which operations apply; the operations enforce order and assert effect.**
Ordering lives as a *precondition an operation refuses to proceed without*, never as a step the
skill is trusted to remember. The consequence is the point: invoking them out of order fails
loudly whether the caller is the skill, a person, a make target, or a different agent.
Correctness stops depending on the skill being read, current, or followed.

Operations are tagged by stack — `guard`, `resolver-block`, `beads`, `verify` are
stack-agnostic; `linter-preset` is python+uv. Only python+uv is implemented; the tag is the seam
a second stack would attach to, and building the abstraction now for a stack that doesn't exist
is what the constitution forbids.

**Trigger:** none — this is active work, blocked only on shelf-efh (the `guard` operation is
`tools/hooks/install.py` and must verify correctly before anything depends on it).

Proposal: openspec/changes/onboard-consumer-skill/

Re-scopes shelf-abf: `make bootstrap` becomes one caller of these operations rather than a
competing implementation. Its contract work (idempotent/ordered/verifying/honest) survives — it
describes the operations instead of a Make target.

Distinct from shelf-c2s (the `catalog`/`onboard` skill), which is the **supply** side: getting
micro-software into the catalog, four entry paths. That stays deferred.

title: Prescribe make bootstrap: onboarding as an enforced target, not a runbook walk
description:
**Problem.** `docs/runbooks/adopt-beads.md` is ~300 lines, and every line of it is either an
ordering constraint or a verification obligation — the two things prose cannot enforce. Three
adoptions have each discovered a new way to get it wrong, and each fix added a paragraph asking
the next agent to be more careful. That does not converge.

Adopting beads on shelf produced four defects in one session, each defeating a runbook rule that
was actually followed: `bd init` seizing `core.hooksPath` and killing the commit guard; a
`git reset --hard` silently reverting `bd config set`; beads and the pre-commit framework
contending for one hook slot; and the guard reporting a checkmark while provably dead.

**Shape of a fix.** Stop writing instructions for an agent to follow; prescribe a target the repo
runs. `make bootstrap` is idempotent, encodes ordering as prerequisites, asserts the effects it
intended (never the artifacts it wrote), and reports live / not-live / could-not-check as three
distinct outcomes. `make bootstrap-verify` joins `make check`, so decay fails the build instead
of going unnoticed. The beads runbook keeps every finding but converts its voice from
instructions-to-a-reader into assertions-a-target-makes.

**Trigger:** none needed — this is active work, blocked only on sequencing.

Blocked by shelf-efh: that change produces the first real verify-by-behavior implementation this
one generalizes. Landing the contract first would prescribe a pattern with no working instance,
which is the "do NOT build on spec" the constitution warns against.

Proposal: openspec/changes/bootstrap-target-contract/
Closes shelf-gag if design D4 (make check depends on bootstrap-verify) lands as proposed.
notes: Re-scoped 2026-08-12 by shelf-n63: make bootstrap cannot bootstrap greenfield (it assumes a Makefile that onboarding produces). Inverted — this now depends on shelf-n63's operation set and becomes one caller of it, not a competing implementation. The contract work (idempotent/ordered/verifying/honest) survives; it describes the operations rather than a Make target. Proposal needs updating when shelf-n63 lands.

title: Commit guard is silently dead when core.hooksPath is set
description:
**Problem.** `tools/hooks/install.py` writes the guard to `<git-dir>/hooks/pre-commit`, a
hardcoded path (line 52: `hooks = git_dir / "hooks"`). It never consults
`git config core.hooksPath`. When a repo sets `core.hooksPath`, git stops reading
`.git/hooks` entirely — so the installer reports success, the file exists, and the guard
never fires.

**Evidence (verified 2026-08-12, this repo, not inferred).** `bd init` sets
`core.hooksPath = .beads/hooks`. A probe hook written to `.git/hooks/pre-commit` containing
`exit 1` did **not** block a commit — the commit succeeded cleanly. The `.beads/hooks/*`
shims contain only bd's own marker-delimited block; they do not chain through to any
pre-existing hook.

**Scope is wider than beads.** `husky`, `lefthook`, and the `pre-commit` framework all set
`core.hooksPath` the same way. Any consumer using any of them has a silently-dead shelf
guard today.

**Relationship to the per-clone gap:** distinct. That one is "unarmed until you run the
installer". This one is "disarmed *even after* you run it" — strictly worse, because the
installer's success message makes it look armed.

**Shape of a fix:** resolve the hook directory as
`git rev-parse --git-path hooks` (which honors `core.hooksPath`) instead of
`git_dir / "hooks"`. If the resolved directory is foreign-managed (a beads/husky/lefthook
shim already present), the existing "refuses to clobber a foreign one" branch should either
chain the guard in or fail loudly — deciding which is part of this issue.

Found while adopting beads on shelf (docs/runbooks/adopt-beads.md); the runbook needs this
recorded as a Phase 1 gap.
notes: Rescoped by shelf-gag (ledger 0085, 2026-08-12): enforcement now lives in `make check` via the new `guard` target, which reads HEAD and needs no hooks. This bug is therefore no longer a safety hole — it is fast feedback that lies. Still worth fixing: an installer that reports success while installing a dead hook is its own defect, and the proposal's verify-by-behavior work is the pattern shelf-n63 builds on.

title: Guard enforcement is per-clone — a fresh clone is unguarded
description:
Onboarding installs the hook in one command (`tools/hooks/install.py`,
docs/consuming-the-shelf.md §2), but git hooks can't be committed, so a fresh clone is
unguarded until someone runs it.

**Trigger:** a 2nd machine/clone, OR the first leaked override — then fold a working-tree
check into `make check` (or enforce in CI).

Migrated from docs/backlog.md § "Gaps".

---

**Re-scoped 2026-08-12, and promoted to the primary fix.** The original framing treated the
hook as the enforcement mechanism and a `make check` check as a fallback. That is backwards,
and this repo demonstrates why: `forbid-local-shelf-source.py` is invoked by **nothing except
the pre-commit hook** — not `make check`, not the test suite. So the single enforcement path
was a per-clone, silently-disableable artifact, and it was in fact dead here (shelf-efh).

Two different things were conflated:

- **The assertion** — "no local `path=`/editable shelf source in this repo's content." A
  property of the repo. Cheap, deterministic, true or false anywhere, needs no hooks and no
  onboarding. This belongs in `make check`.
- **The mechanism** — a pre-commit hook. Per-clone, disableable by any tool that claims
  `core.hooksPath`, and invisible when broken. Useful only as *fast feedback*: you learn at
  commit time instead of at `make check` time.

**Shape of a fix:** add a `guard` target to `make check` that runs the existing
`forbid-local-shelf-source.py` against the working tree. No new logic — the script exists and
is verified (ledger 0038); it has simply never been wired to the gate.

This inverts the risk. Once the assertion is in `make check`, a dead hook costs latency, not
safety — which makes shelf-efh a real bug but no longer a hole, and makes shelf-abf's
hook-liveness verification a convenience rather than a safety-critical check.

**No longer blocked.** It was briefly filed behind shelf-efh and shelf-abf; that was wrong.
This is the cheapest and highest-value of the three and depends on neither. Do it first.

**Note: this repo has no CI** (no `.github/workflows/`). The original "or enforce in CI"
alternative has nothing to attach to — `make check` is the only gate that exists.

touches a2web's live path.

**Shape of a fix:** a `WORKFLOW: BENCH` run (resolution 0011) with a real-web corpus is the
proper treatment.

**Trigger:** build when it matters.

— pandoc dropped for mammoth.

title: No CI: the Definition of Done is enforced only by whoever remembers to run it
description:
**Problem.** This repo has no CI of any kind — no `.github/workflows/`, no GitLab/Circle/Travis
config. Verified 2026-08-12. Yet `AGENTS.md` states the Definition of Done in the strongest
terms available: `make check` green across the **entire repo**, "**No carve-outs.** 'Pre-existing
drift', 'unrelated file', or 'that's a separate change' do **not** satisfy Done."

Nothing enforces that. A commit can reach `main` having never run it. The rule is aspirational,
and its aspiration is invisible — a violation looks exactly like compliance.

**Evidence from this session (2026-08-12), which is the reason this is filed at all.**

- The commit guard was dead for an unknown period (shelf-efh). It was found only because an
  unrelated beads adoption happened to probe it. No standing mechanism would ever have surfaced
  it — because there is no standing mechanism.
- shelf-gag's own recorded fix says "fold a working-tree check into `make check` (or enforce in
  CI)". The second alternative has nothing to attach to. That was written as if a choice
  existed; it doesn't.
- Two uncommitted work streams were sitting in the tree with `make check` red (a `D301`, two
  import-sort errors, a codespell hit, four missing `ty` ignores). Locally caught, but only
  because someone ran the gate before committing. Nothing required that.
- The `PROMOTE` workflow (agent-loop.md) does its work in a **git worktree** and merges to
  `main`. A worktree is a fresh checkout — per-clone hooks do not exist there unless installed,
  which nobody does mid-promotion.

**Shape of a fix.** Minimal and cheap: one GitHub Actions workflow running `make check` on push
and pull request. Note the browser tests are already a separate target (`make test-browser`), so
the gate needs no browser engines — `make check` is 751 tests, ~45s locally, and needs only uv.

**The fair counter-argument, recorded so this can be deferred with evidence rather than
re-litigated.** Single contributor, single machine. This repo already defers `release-please`
(shelf-0aw) pending "a 2nd tag/changelog bookkeeping mistake, OR a 2nd human contributor" on
exactly that reasoning, and CI's marginal value scales the same way. At n=1 the gate is
"whatever the one person runs", and they do run it.

**Why it may still be worth it at n=1:** the failure this session found was not a person
forgetting to run the gate — it was a guarantee that silently stopped holding while every
signal said it held. That class of failure is invisible to discipline, however good, because
discipline checks the things you remember to check. A second, non-local execution of the gate
is the cheapest thing that observes the repo from outside its own assumptions.

**One honest complication.** The property-based suites added 2026-08-12 run 300 randomized
Hypothesis examples per test per run, and `.hypothesis/` is self-gitignored — so CI would
explore a different input space than any local run. That is a feature (it finds real boundaries;
`ms=1450` was found exactly this way) and a liability (a latent boundary fails an unrelated PR).
Decide `derandomize` / seeding policy as part of standing up CI, not after the first red build
on someone else's change. See docs/runbooks/property-based-testing.md.

Related: shelf-gag (its "or enforce in CI" alternative), shelf-efh, shelf-abf.

title: a2web adopts anyllm.ProviderName (decided direction, unbuilt)
description:
`anyllm-v0.3.0` (ledger 0037) added a `StrEnum` on the shelf side; a2web's plugin-registry
keys (`"anthropic"`, `"claude-code"`) and `ProviderMode` Literal (`settings.py:30`) are a
*different* string set — not cosmetic drift, so this isn't a mechanical rename.

**Decided 2026-07-09: adopt, not just align** — that's the only way to get drift-safety on
future anyllm releases. Reasoning, for the a2web session that picks this up:

- Bumping anyllm's pin alone can't force a2web to notice a new provider —
  `build_adapter(provider: str, ...)` stays loosely typed *on purpose* (it's a
  config-ingestion boundary; YAML/env are always strings, so `ty` can't help there, and the
  function already validates at runtime). Static drift-detection has to live in the
  *consumer's* typed code, not the library's boundary function.
- The fix: a2web parses its config string into `ProviderName` **once**, at the settings field
  itself — `ProviderMode = Literal[...]` → `provider: ProviderName` on the
  `pydantic_settings.BaseSettings` field. `StrEnum` is natively a pydantic validator; no
  custom `field_validator` needed. Everything downstream in a2web becomes `ProviderName`-typed
  for free.
- Payoff: an exhaustive `match`/`case` (`assert_never` on the fallback, no wildcard) anywhere
  downstream then gets `ty`-checked — a future anyllm provider added without a matching a2web
  branch fails typecheck on `make check`, not silently at runtime.
- The one real design decision buried in the rename: a2web's plugin registry currently has
  **one** `"claude-code"` plugin where anyllm distinguishes `CLAUDE_CODE_CLI` vs
  `CLAUDE_CODE_SDK` — decide whether a2web wants both exposed as separate plugins or
  deliberately collapses them, don't let the rename paper over that.
- `PluginManifest.name` is a public lookup key (`registry["anthropic"]`) — ships as a breaking
  change, per `RECEIVE` step 4 ("migrate to the new idiom, not the smallest diff... delete
  compat shims").

**Note:** the work itself lands in the a2web repo, not shelf. Tracked here because shelf owns
the `anyllm` side of the contract.

Migrated from docs/backlog.md § "Decide — open forks (a decision, not a build)".

title: forbid-local-shelf-source.py crashes with uncaught traceback on malformed pyproject.toml
description:
The guard (tools/hooks/forbid-local-shelf-source.py) calls tomllib.loads(content)
with no exception handling in both _staged_pyproject/_committed_pyproject read
paths. A malformed pyproject.toml -- e.g. a duplicate [tool.uv.sources] table,
which is invalid TOML -- crashes with an uncaught tomllib.TOMLDecodeError
traceback instead of the guard's own clean stderr message.

Found for real 2026-08-12: an accidental duplicate [tool.uv.sources] table
(from an unrelated live-fire test of the guard that leaked into a real commit)
made the guard crash on every invocation, staged and committed alike, on
shelf's own pyproject.toml.

Not currently dangerous: an uncaught exception's default exit code is 1, same
as "offenders found," so this is accidentally fail-closed rather than
fail-open -- a malformed file still blocks the commit/gate. But it's not
intentional, no test in tests/test_guard.py covers this path, and the
operator sees a raw Python traceback instead of the guard's own designed
error message ("NOT a pass" framing etc).

Shape of a fix (not researched): wrap the tomllib.loads call in a try/except
tomllib.TOMLDecodeError, print a guard-styled error to stderr (consistent
with the existing "could not check" / exit-2 framing for the not-a-git-repo
case -- arguably malformed TOML deserves the same COULD_NOT_CHECK=2 treatment
rather than exit 1, since the guard genuinely could not evaluate the file, as
distinct from evaluating it and finding an offender), and add a test case
(a repo with a deliberately malformed/duplicate-table pyproject.toml) to
tests/test_guard.py alongside the existing outside-a-git-repo case.

Found during a shelf-runbook review session cross-checking the adopt-beads
runbook's homelab/shelf adoption findings (see docs/runbooks/adopt-beads.md).
